newsitem.title: UK: Japan suffers share pain but no debt gain.
newsitem.headline: Japan suffers share pain but no debt gain.

text.p: Japanese government bonds have benefited heartily from the stock market's descent but the rally is unlikely to entice foreigners, analysts said on Monday.
There is an argument for buying Japanese government bonds (JGBs) as protection against any U.S. interest rate rise but further yen weakness is likely to neutralise such a play.

"What's bad for the Nikkei is good news for JGBs but with close to historical lows in yield terms, it's very difficult to see JGBs sustaining further significant gains," said Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London.

Japan's Nikkei average of 225 leading shares slumped 3.37 percent on Monday, pulling the index down to a close of 17,480.34 from the year's open of 19,364.24, amid concerns about the sickly economy and pending financial reforms.
The plunge has sent domestic investors scurrying for cover to the government bond market, pushing down the yield on 10-year bonds to 2.4 percent on Monday, near historic lows.
The JGB futures market has also soared, hitting a high of 126.32 in Tokyo on Monday, just off an all-time high of 126.58.
But analysts said foreign investors were likely to continue to shun such low yields, despite the price gains.
Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International in London, said that JGBs looked good on paper. "If you're looking at pure price performance it will outperform the U.S.," he said.
News from Japan on Monday that Kyotaru Co Ltd, a chain of sushi restaurants, had filed for insolvency, showed banks were no longer in a position to bail out ailing companies.
Kyotaru is the first firm listed on the first section of the Tokyo Stock Exchange to fail since mid-1993.
Hannah added Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's vow earlier in the day to go ahead with tax rises and financial reform meant the pain in the equity market was likely to continue.
"You're left with a tightening fiscal scenario, not much that can be done on monetary policy except to leave interest rates unchanged, and equities still plunging," he said.
Such a picture supported bonds, Hannah said. There was a risk the Nikkei-225 could revisit its 1995 lows of around 14,500 bringing a 2.25 percent yield on 10-year bonds within reach.
But he added, "From a foreign perspective it's totally neutralised by further potential weakness in the yen."
The dollar hit a 46-month high against the yen of 118.18 on Monday. Hannah said IBJ had a dollar/yen target of 120.00. "Hedging out the risk would be enormous and it wouldn't be worth it," he said.
Andrew Bevan, senior bond economist at Goldman Sachs in London, said JGBs were a good choice as a shield against any interest rate rise from the U.S. Federal Reserve.

Goldman Sachs expected a rise in March, he said. "Whereas the European markets might get hurt if the Fed tightens policy as we expect them to do... we don't think that would be so disturbing for Japan which is trading independently," he said.
At the same time, Japanese interest rates were likely to remain on hold as stock market uncertainty continued, he said.
"From a portfolio prespective you might be able to find something encouraging to say," Bevan said.
